chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Mahboub, from Salih ibn Sahl, from Kirdayn, from a man, from Abu Abdillah and Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, when Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) finished with the people of Basra, seventy men from the Zut came to him. They greeted him and spoke to him in their language, so he responded to them in their language. Then he said to them: 'I am not as you say; I am a servant of Allah, a created being.' But they refused him and said, 'You are He.' So he said to them: 'If you do not cease and retract from what you said about me, and repent to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, I will surely kill you.'

So they refused to retract and repent. He ordered wells to be dug for them, and they were dug. Then he made holes connecting some to others, then threw them into them. Then he covered their tops, then fire was kindled in one of the wells that had no one from them in it. So the smoke entered upon them in it, and they died.

key_terms.أَنْتَ هُوَ: You are He (a phrase of deification)
key_terms.الزُّط: A group known for extreme beliefs (Ghulat)

ai.seo_question: What happened to the Zut when they refused to repent after claiming divinity for Imam Ali (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the historical context of the Ghulat (extremists) who attributed divinity to Imam Ali (AS) following the Battle of the Camel, a key moment in early Shia theological development. Upon their refusal to repent despite his invitation, Imam Ali executed the penalty of strangulation via smoke (kaff al-dukhan) in interconnected wells, a method distinct from the sword execution often cited for apostates. This event underscores the practical application of hadd penalties in the Imamate era and serves as a primary reference for the status of the Zut in Shia jurisprudence.
